subChunks.title: Requests for Comments: Driving Alignment Through Written Design
subChunks.hookHtml: The RFC (Request for Comments) is how Lead engineers drive significant technical change through an organisation without either unilaterally imposing decisions or spending weeks in endless meetings. A well-written RFC builds shared understanding, surfaces objections early, and produces a documented decision that new engineers can read years later. Most engineers know what an RFC is; few know how to write one that actually gets the right decision made.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
When to Write an RFC

Not every decision needs an RFC. RFCs are appropriate for: changes that affect more than one team, decisions with significant irreversibility, changes to core architectural patterns, migrations that require coordination across services, and decisions where reasonable engineers might make different choices. Signs you need an RFC: if the decision will be made in a meeting with no written artefact, it is probably too important for that. If you can make the decision and reverse it without major cost, an RFC is overhead.

RFC Structure

A good RFC answers, in order:

  1. Summary / TL;DR: one paragraph — what are you proposing and why? Readers decide whether to engage based on this.
  2. Motivation / Problem: what problem are you solving? Not the solution — the problem. Readers need to agree that the problem is worth solving before evaluating your solution.
  3. Current state: what is the status quo? Why is it insufficient? Evidence, data, concrete examples of the problem manifesting.
  4. Proposal: your recommended approach. Specific enough to evaluate, not so detailed it's an implementation spec. Diagrams help. Trade-offs acknowledged.
  5. Alternatives considered: at least two alternatives with specific reasons they were not chosen. Demonstrates rigour and pre-empts 'what about X?' comments.
  6. Impact: what teams/services are affected? What is the migration path? What is the rollout plan?
  7. Open questions: things you haven't resolved. Asking explicitly is better than leaving gaps that reviewers find.
  8. Appendix: detailed technical specs, data, benchmarks — for those who want depth without making the main RFC dense.

The Review Process

An RFC's review period should be explicit — 'comments by Friday, decision by next Wednesday' — not open-ended. Open-ended review periods are never closed. The author drives the process: responds to comments, summarises discussion, and makes the final call (with escalation path for unresolved disagreement).

RFC review modes: approve (I support this), comment (I have a question or concern but am not blocking), request changes (I believe there is a significant gap that must be addressed before this proceeds). The decision process should be explicit — is this a single-decider RFC or a consensus RFC?

Writing for Readers Who Disagree

The most common RFC failure: writing a persuasion document rather than a decision document. If your RFC reads like a sales pitch for your solution, readers who have doubts become adversaries rather than collaborators. Write to surface the strongest version of each alternative, acknowledge the real downsides of your proposal, and frame the question as 'given these trade-offs, here is why I believe this is the right path' — not 'here is why I am right.'

Pre-empt objections by raising them yourself: 'You might wonder why we're not choosing X — here is why.' This disarms the objection and demonstrates you've thought it through. An RFC that anticipates and answers the hard questions is much harder to block than one that pretends they don't exist.

Making RFCs Stick

An RFC that produces a decision but is never referenced again has not succeeded. The decision from an RFC should be recorded as an ADR (Architecture Decision Record) in the codebase. The RFC document is the deliberation; the ADR is the conclusion. Future engineers should be able to find both: the decision and the reasoning process that produced it.

storyBeats.text: The Lead had been trying to move the team off their homegrown HTTP client for three months. Two design reviews had been inconclusive. A Slack thread with 140 messages had produced no decision. She wrote an RFC: current state, why it's a problem, her proposal, two alternatives, the trade-off matrix, open questions. She posted it on Monday with a 'comments by Thursday, decision by Friday' deadline. By Wednesday there were 12 substantive comments. By Friday the team had agreed, with two modifications to the proposal. The decision that three months of meetings hadn't produced, one week of async writing delivered.

storyBeats.speaker: Principal Engineer Iolo
storyBeats.text: The RFC that reads like a persuasion document will always generate more resistance than one that reads like a careful analysis. When you read an RFC and it presents only one good option and strawmans the alternatives, you immediately become suspicious — what is the author not telling you? When you read an RFC that presents the alternatives fairly, acknowledges the genuine downsides of the proposal, and says 'given these trade-offs, here is my recommendation and why' — you feel like you are reading something honest. Trust that document more, not less.

storyBeats.speaker: Principal Engineer Iolo
storyBeats.text: The open questions section is the most underused part of an RFC template. Authors fear that listing things they haven't resolved makes them look underprepared. The opposite is true. An RFC with an explicit open questions section says: 'I know what I know and I know what I don't know.' It invites reviewers to contribute to the parts that are unresolved rather than pointing out gaps as if the author hadn't noticed them. The RFC becomes collaborative rather than defensive.

storyBeats.speaker: Principal Engineer Iolo
storyBeats.text: Set a deadline for comments and honour it. An RFC with a vague 'please comment' invitation will never close. 'Comments by Thursday 5pm; I will update the proposal based on feedback and post the final decision by Monday' — that is a process. Reviewers know when to engage. The author knows when to wrap up. The team knows when to expect the outcome. The decision gets made. Without deadlines, RFCs become eternal documents that are simultaneously unresolved and irrelevant.

learningObjectives: Identify the situations that warrant an RFC vs those that do not
Write a complete RFC structure with all eight sections including alternatives considered and open questions
Explain why 'persuasion document' RFCs generate more resistance than honest trade-off analysis
Describe the RFC review process including explicit deadlines, review modes, and decision documentation
commonMistakes: Writing an RFC as a sales pitch for a predetermined conclusion rather than an honest trade-off analysis
Leaving the review period open-ended — RFCs without deadlines are never closed
Omitting the 'alternatives considered' section — signals the author hasn't thought through other options
Failing to record the RFC decision as an ADR — the decision becomes undiscoverable for future engineers
assessmentCriteria: Can identify whether a given scenario warrants an RFC or a simpler decision process
Can write a complete RFC skeleton with all eight sections for a real technical decision
Can take an RFC that reads as a persuasion document and identify specifically what makes it adversarial rather than collaborative
Can define a review process with explicit deadline, review modes, and documentation path
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a Senior engineer why 'just making a decision and telling the team' is often wrong for significant technical changes, and why an RFC is better. What does an RFC produce that a meeting doesn't? What makes the difference between an RFC that builds alignment and one that creates more conflict?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Write the following sections of an RFC for this scenario:

Scenario: The Academy currently runs all services as a single monolithic Spring Boot application. You are proposing to extract the payment processing functionality into a separate service. Write: (1) A TL;DR summary (one paragraph). (2) The motivation and problem section. (3) Two alternatives considered with specific reasons they were rejected. (4) Three open questions.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. TL;DR:
We propose extracting payment processing from the monolith into an independent service by Q3. Payment processing has materially different compliance requirements (PCI DSS), a different scaling profile from the rest of the application, and incidents in the payment path are currently coupled to the spell and user features. A dedicated payment service allows independent deployment, scoped PCI scope reduction, and a clearer ownership boundary. This RFC proposes the extraction approach, migration path, and team ownership model.

2. Motivation / Problem:
Payment processing in the monolith creates three problems:
(a) PCI compliance scope: PCI DSS requirements apply to all systems that touch cardholder data. Currently, because payment code lives in the monolith, all of our services and engineers are technically in scope for PCI audit requirements, even those that never touch payment flows. Isolation would reduce PCI scope to a single service.
(b) Deployment coupling: three incidents in the past 6 months have been caused by payment-unrelated deployments triggering a restart that interrupted in-flight payment transactions. The most recent cost £4,200 in processing fees from retry-related double-charges.
(c) Team cognitive load: the Academy team currently owns payment logic alongside spell management, user accounts, and content — three separate domains with very different risk profiles. The payment code requires specific knowledge (idempotency keys, retry handling, webhook verification) that is diluted when it is one module among many.

3. Alternatives Considered:
(a) Modular monolith with better boundary enforcement:
Pro: no operational overhead of a separate service; no network calls between payment and the rest of the application. Con: does not reduce PCI scope — if code is in the same deployment, it remains in scope. Does not solve the deployment coupling problem — a monolith restart still affects payment transactions. Does not allow independent scaling. Rejected because it does not address the PCI scope reduction goal, which is the highest-priority driver.

(b) Use a fully managed payment processor (e.g., Stripe without a custom service wrapper):
Pro: no service to maintain; PCI compliance largely offloaded to Stripe. Con: the Academy has complex custom pricing logic that is not well-served by Stripe's standard webhooks; we have already invested 18 months in the custom billing logic and the business is not willing to migrate that logic to a third party. The custom logic will remain regardless. Rejected because it does not address the real problem — we will always have payment logic, the question is where it lives.

4. Open Questions:
(a) Transaction consistency: currently, spell unlock and payment recording are done in the same database transaction. If we extract payment to a separate service, this is no longer possible. The RFC currently proposes a saga pattern for consistency — but we haven't designed the compensation logic for the 'payment succeeded, spell unlock failed' case. This needs to be designed before extraction begins.
(b) Team ownership: should the payment service be owned by the existing team (adding a second service to their ownership) or should we staff a dedicated payment team? The RFC proposes the latter, but this is a resourcing decision that needs VP approval.
(c) Gradual rollout: can we extract payment processing behind a feature flag, routing a percentage of payment requests through the new service while the monolith handles the rest? Or does the PCI scope reduction only apply once 100% of traffic routes through the new service?
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: The Academy is deciding whether to move from a single PostgreSQL database (shared by all services) to per-service databases. This is a significant architectural decision with clear benefits and clear costs. Write a complete RFC for this decision: all eight sections (Summary, Motivation, Current State, Proposal, Alternatives Considered, Impact, Open Questions, Appendix outline). The RFC should be honest about the genuine trade-offs — not a sales pitch for one side.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
RFC: Per-Service Database Isolation
Status: Draft | Author: [Lead] | Review deadline: [Date + 7 days] | Decision expected: [Date + 10 days]

1. Summary / TL;DR:
We currently operate a single PostgreSQL database shared across all four services (spell, user, tournament, payment). We propose migrating to per-service databases over a 9-month period. This increases deployment independence, reduces blast radius of schema changes, and enables service-appropriate database choices. The cost is increased operational complexity and the loss of cross-service joins. This RFC presents the trade-offs and asks for a decision on whether to proceed.

2. Motivation / Problem:
- Schema coupling: a migration that changes the users table requires coordination with every service that queries it. Three sprint delays in the last quarter were caused by cross-service migration coordination.
- Blast radius: a DBA error or runaway query on the spell table can degrade connections for the payment service — these are completely unrelated workloads.
- Scaling: tournament leaderboard queries are read-heavy with different indexes needed from user authentication queries. In a shared database, index strategy is a compromise.

3. Current State:
All four services use the same PostgreSQL instance (Neon). The connection pool is shared. Schema migrations run via Flyway from a shared migrations folder. Cross-service foreign key references exist in 3 places. The database has grown to 45GB with different growth rates per domain (tournament data growing 40% quarter-on-quarter; user data growing linearly).

4. Proposal:
Migrate to 4 PostgreSQL databases (one per service) over 9 months, in phases:
- Phase 1 (months 1–3): Extract payment database (highest compliance priority; fewest cross-service joins). Use event publishing for consistency — payment service emits EntitlementGranted event; other services consume.
- Phase 2 (months 4–6): Extract tournament database. Address leaderboard read scaling with a read replica.
- Phase 3 (months 7–9): Extract user and spell databases, the most coupled pair. Remove remaining cross-service foreign keys. Final shared database decommissioned.
Each phase includes data migration scripts, parallel read period for validation, cutover, and original table archiving.

5. Alternatives Considered:
(a) Logical schemas within the same database instance (PostgreSQL schemas):
Provides some isolation (per-schema connection users, per-schema GRANT statements) without full database separation. Pro: no data migration; maintains cross-schema joins. Con: does not solve scaling (same connection pool, same resource limits); does not enable different database technologies per service; PCI scope reduction requires true network isolation, not logical schema separation. Rejected because it does not achieve the compliance or scaling goals.
(b) Keep the shared database but enforce access rules via an API gateway pattern:
Services only access their own data through a domain API; no direct cross-service SQL. Pro: no migration cost. Con: existing code has widespread direct SQL access; refactoring all cross-service data access to API calls is similar in cost to database extraction but without the scaling and compliance benefits. Rejected as highest-cost option with lowest benefit.

6. Impact:
- All four service teams are affected: each team will own their database migration and will need to replace 2–3 cross-service joins with API calls or event subscriptions.
- SRE team will manage 4 database instances instead of 1 (Neon makes this manageable with branching).
- Rollout is phased — no team is blocked during any phase.
- Estimated engineering effort: 3 weeks per service pair (migration + join refactoring + testing). Total: ~12 weeks of engineering time spread across 9 months.

7. Open Questions:
(a) Referential integrity: we currently have a tournament_results.user_id foreign key referencing users.id. After extraction, this constraint cannot be enforced at the database level. What is the agreed approach for handling orphaned references? (Options: soft deletion with retention period, application-level consistency check, event-driven cleanup).
(b) Reporting queries: the analytics team runs weekly cross-service JOIN queries (tournament results joined with user profile data). These will break after extraction. Do we build a read-aggregation service, a data warehouse ETL, or a reporting replica that replicates from all four databases?
(c) Cost: 4 separate Neon projects will have different billing implications. Finance team needs to confirm budget before we commit to Phase 1.

8. Appendix:
- Appendix A: List of all cross-service foreign keys and proposed resolution for each
- Appendix B: Data volume by table and projected growth (basis for per-service scaling decisions)
- Appendix C: Neon per-project pricing analysis
- Appendix D: Draft data migration scripts for Phase 1 (payment service extraction)

questions.questionHtml: Why is the 'Alternatives Considered' section important in an RFC?
options: It pads the document to make it seem more thorough
It demonstrates that the author has genuinely evaluated other options and pre-empts 'what about X?' objections from reviewers
It is only needed for RFCs that affect more than two teams
It allows reviewers to vote on which alternative they prefer
questions.correctAnswer: It demonstrates that the author has genuinely evaluated other options and pre-empts 'what about X?' objections from reviewers
questions.explanationHtml: Reviewers who have thought about a problem will almost always have considered alternatives. An RFC without an alternatives section invites the comment 'but have you thought about Y?' — which stalls the review and makes the RFC seem underprepared. An alternatives section that presents each option fairly and explains specifically why it was not chosen pre-empts these objections, builds trust in the author's reasoning, and elevates the quality of discussion to 'given these constraints, is this the right trade-off?' rather than 'you didn't even consider the obvious alternative.'

questions.questionHtml: An RFC about migrating to a new authentication library has been in review for 3 weeks with no decision. New comments keep arriving. What is the most likely cause and how should the author respond?
options: The RFC is too complex — it should be split into multiple smaller RFCs
The review period was never bounded — there is no deadline, so comments arrive indefinitely and no decision is ever forced
The team doesn't care about authentication
The RFC needs more technical detail to resolve the discussion
questions.correctAnswer: The review period was never bounded — there is no deadline, so comments arrive indefinitely and no decision is ever forced
questions.explanationHtml: Open-ended review periods never close. Without a deadline, every new reader can add more comments, every comment spawns more discussion, and no one is responsible for making the decision. The fix: the author sets an explicit deadline ('comments by [date], decision by [date+3 days]'), responds to all open comments, summarises any significant unresolved disagreement, and posts the decision. If there is unresolved disagreement that the author cannot resolve, they escalate to their manager or the relevant decision-maker rather than waiting for consensus to emerge organically.

questions.questionHtml: An RFC should primarily serve as a persuasion document that presents the strongest possible case for the author's preferred solution.
questions.explanationHtml: An RFC written as a persuasion document generates more resistance, not less. When readers can see that alternatives are strawmanned or that genuine downsides are omitted, they become suspicious of the analysis and more likely to object. An effective RFC is an honest trade-off analysis: present each alternative fairly, acknowledge the real downsides of your proposal, and frame the decision as 'given these constraints, here is my recommendation and the reasoning.' Readers who trust the analysis are more likely to support the decision, even if they would have preferred a different outcome.
